title: Global powers converge on Manila as ASEAN summit kicks off
html:
ASEAN nation leaders and representatives join hands for a group photo during the opening of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits at the Philippine International Convention Center in Manila, on Nov 15.

ST PHOTO: GAVIN FOO

AI generated

MANILA – A key regional summit opened on Nov 15 in Manila, with South-east Asian heads of state facing questions on trade, security and an ongoing energy crisis while playing host to a “who’s who” of global leaders.

US President Donald Trump is scheduled to arrive on Nov 17 near the summit’s conclusion, a visit expected to include a sideline meeting with fellow Quad countries India, Japan and Australia – the first of his second term.

The meeting of the Quad – a grouping broadly aimed at counterbalancing China’s regional influence – would come days before a historic sit-down with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen.

Brazil’s recently re-elected Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, meanwhile, is set to attend a plenary session of the 11-member ASEAN on Nov 15, while Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will sign a new defence pact with host country the Philippines.

Nearly 20,000 police officers have been deployed around Metro Manila for the summit, with progressive groups predicting a turnout of thousands on Nov 17 for an anti-Trump march at the summit site.

Much of the uproar targets the US Pax Silica programme – a supply-chain initiative designed to counter China’s dominance in semiconductors and rare earths – whose flagship Philippine project, a 1,620ha artificial intelligence manufacturing hub north of Manila, threatens to displace indigenous families.

US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton said last week that a widely rumoured November target date for a deal signing timed with Trump’s visit was never in the works.

Unfinished business

A day of early meetings kicked off on Nov 14 with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announcing a Philippine trade deal, and ASEAN leaders huddling on key issues including haze from Indonesia and potential fuel-sharing schemes as members struggle with Iran war-driven shortages.

But two issues that have vexed ASEAN leaders for years – a languishing South China Sea “Code of Conduct” and ASEAN’s relationship with war-torn Myanmar – look to be Singapore’s problem when the grouping’s rotating chair passes to the city-state in 2027.

Myanmar has been excluded from high-level ASEAN meetings since a 2021 military coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and triggered an ongoing civil war.

Thailand, which shares a border with Myanmar and is leading the charge for closer relations, last week called for Naypyitaw’s Foreign Minister to be allowed back into meetings.

But Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro told reporters on Nov 14 there was “no easing” of the approach being taken with Myanmar, which faces an international ruling on whether it committed genocide against its marginalised Muslim Rohingya minority.

Hopes of achieving a so-called Code of Conduct in the disputed South China Sea between ASEAN states and China during Manila’s year in the chair, meanwhile, have flagged.

A South-east Asian diplomat involved in summit preparations said he did not expect a code to be signed at the summit.

Lazaro indicated as much on Nov 14, saying negotiations were “80%” complete.

“If it happens, then it’s a small miracle,” said Siew Mun Tang, former head of the ASEAN Studies Centre at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute.

Shadow of Beijing

Beijing claims most of the South China Sea despite an international ruling that its assertion has no legal basis, and its coast guard has clashed repeatedly with that of the Philippines.

The row has reared its head at inopportune times over the past year, with a July foreign ministers’ summit opening less than a day after Chinese and Philippine sailors engaged in a clash.

An ASEAN defence chiefs meeting in October saw Beijing sending only an embassy defence attache, blaming “reckless” statements by Philippine politicians.

A week later, Manila issued a rare rebuke to its own public officials over comments about China, stressing the need for a unified voice as the two countries negotiate.

As the summit opens on Nov 15, an annual seminar less than 5km away will be making the case against China’s South China Sea claims.

Philippine defence chief Gilberto Teodoro, sanctioned by Beijing in 2026 for what it called “irresponsible remarks”, will give a keynote address. AFP
summary: US President Donald Trump is scheduled to arrive on Nov 17 near the summit’s conclusion.
